You can think Black Lives Matter is a deeply confused and destructive movement, and still pity this family. I do, anyway. Mr. Castile does not appear to be a thug like Michael Brown or Trayvon Martin. If he really has a concealed weapon permit, it is important that he can inform an officer that he is armed without being killed for doing so. This is true for people of all races.

From a 2nd Amendment perspective, I'm curious to hear the officer's side of events, whether he just heard the phrase "I'm armed" and saw a black dude and panicked, or whether there was some other instigating conduct that would've made his shot justifiable. I wish people -- liberals, especially -- could acknowledge they don't have the full set of facts yet, and separate their emotional response from their political response, but... I'm not holding my breath.

To me, that's the real issue in all of this.

Our political dialogue in this country is driven by viral videos instead of statistics and facts.

Chicago has over 60 people shot in a weekend, but the ones doing the shooting aren't livestreaming it to Facebook, so the issue doesn't generate the kind of widespread emotional response a video like this does. If the news doesn't have video to show, it's essentially a non-story. The media wants clicks, pageviews, ratings. You need video for that.

And where can you get a reliable source of emotional video? Cops. Police officers are on video all the time. When they show up to a disturbance, the phones come out immediately. Cops have dash cams, body cams, and security cams all recording their every move. There are roughly 400,000 full-time law enforcement officers in the U.S. and each one engages in dozens of individual calls per shift, 365 days a year.

Out of those billions of public interactions, there are inevitably going to be some heartbreaking catastrophes like this one. There are good cops who make mistakes, and there are bad cops who get caught. But what tiny fraction of a percentage of public interactions do these videos represent? Are they a meaningful trend or just a few dots on a multibillion-pixel canvas? Can we even have a reasonable discussion about this, or are we just supposed to acquiesce to our cities and our democracy being shut down and our Constitutional rights stripped away by political agitators?

Outrage is not an argument. Neither is sympathy. I hear and read all the time about African-Americans who have "The Talk" with their kids about how dangerous law enforcement is, when their kids are far more likely to be killed by people who go to the same schools they do and look just like them. I can grieve for tragedy and still know that the statistics paint a different picture.

Medical billing and coding are two important related facets of the healthcare industry. Both medical billing and medical coding are part of revenue cycle management or the part of healthcare industry that deals with payments to healthcare providers for the services rendered. To make things simple, we will look into the process and aspects of medical coding first before getting into medical billing.The initial purposes of medical coding was to provide morbidity stats to the WHO, verifying the need for patient care and providing statistics helpful to analysis of healthcare costs. Medical coding is now very much relied upon by the insurance industry for reimbursements to medical providers too. The coding processes have been revised from ICD-9 format to the latest ICD-10 format which in turn contains codes which are more extensive and very specific.
